paragraphs: The paper develops an accelerated randomized proximal coordinate gradient method for composite convex optimization. This setting combines parts of an objective that can be handled through gradient and proximal updates. Coordinate methods work with selected portions of the variables, making the cost of individual updates an important consideration alongside the number of updates required.

The main theoretical result concerns strongly convex objectives: the proposed method achieves faster linear convergence rates than existing randomized proximal coordinate gradient methods. Linear convergence describes a recurring proportional reduction in optimization error. The improvement therefore concerns how quickly repeated updates reduce that error under the stated strong convexity condition.

The authors also apply the method to the dual formulation of regularized empirical risk minimization. They develop implementations that avoid operations on full-dimensional vectors, connecting the convergence analysis to computational efficiency. For ill-conditioned empirical risk minimization problems, they establish improved convergence rates over stochastic dual coordinate ascent. This identifies a specific setting where the acceleration offers a theoretical advantage.
neurips-2014-an-accelerated-proximal-coo.tldr: An accelerated coordinate optimization method improves convergence guarantees for strongly convex objectives and ill-conditioned empirical risk minimization.

paragraphs: The paper tackles maximum a posteriori inference in Markov logic networks: finding a most probable assignment of truth values under the model. Its approach uses a compact optimization representation that can group indistinguishable ground atoms. This grouping matters because a single optimization variable can then describe assignments involving multiple atoms.

The authors construct an integer polynomial program by systematically combining lifted decomposition, lifted conditioning, and partial grounding. The resulting representation remains lifted because an integer value can stand for a truth assignment to a collection of indistinguishable atoms. They then convert the polynomial program into an integer linear program, allowing established integer linear programming techniques to solve the encoded inference problem.

Experiments on several benchmark Markov logic networks report substantial improvements in both computational efficiency and solution quality over ground inference and existing methods. These findings support the usefulness of combining compact logical representations with integer optimization. The contribution is both an encoding framework and a practical route from that encoding to available solution techniques.
neurips-2014-an-integer-polynomial-progr.tldr: The paper converts lifted MAP inference into compact integer optimization problems, improving efficiency and solution quality on benchmark Markov logic networks.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models often have posterior distributions that cannot be computed tractably. This paper develops an automated variational method that approximates those posteriors using a mixture of Gaussian distributions. The aim is to make inference practical without requiring a separately derived inference algorithm for every new model.

The authors show that the variational objective and its gradients can be efficiently approximated by sampling from univariate Gaussians. They also derive analytic gradients for Gaussian process hyperparameters regardless of the likelihood. Two proposed covariance parameterizations require a number of parameters that grows linearly with the observation count. Together, these results support efficient gradient optimization through a general-purpose procedure.

The method is evaluated on five models and six benchmark datasets. The authors report performance comparable to exact or specially implemented alternatives, while running orders of magnitude faster than the MCMC approaches considered. These findings support its intended role as a practical tool for investigating Gaussian process models with less model-specific inference work.
neurips-2014-automated-variational-infer.tldr: A Gaussian-mixture variational method automates approximate inference for Gaussian process models and performs efficiently across the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: When an agent is uncertain about its environment, an action can provide both reward and information. Bayes-adaptive planning accounts for this interaction by planning over beliefs about the environment. Its optimal policy considers how reducing uncertainty now could affect rewards later, giving a principled treatment of the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

Computing that solution is typically intractable when the underlying state space is large or continuous. The paper proposes a tractable approximation that combines simulation-based search with a new value function approximation technique. The value approximation generalizes across belief space, allowing the method to share estimates of future value across different states of uncertainty.

The authors report that the approach outperforms prior methods on discrete bandit tasks and simple continuous navigation and control tasks. These results show the practical promise of combining search with belief-space value approximation in the tested settings. The method retains the Bayes-adaptive focus on the future value of information while approximating the computation needed to act on it.
neurips-2014-bayes-adaptive-simulation-b.tldr: Combining simulation-based search with belief-space value approximation makes Bayes-adaptive planning tractable in the tasks studied.

paragraphs: Constrained convex optimization requires progress on two fronts: improving the objective and satisfying the constraints. An intermediate solution can perform well on one measure while still needing improvement on the other. This paper introduces a model-based excessive gap technique for analyzing first-order primal-dual methods with these two goals explicitly separated.

Using the technique, the authors construct methods with optimal convergence rates for both the primal objective residual and the primal feasibility gap. The objective residual measures distance from the optimal objective value, while the feasibility gap measures constraint violation. Separate rate guarantees describe how each quantity improves along the generated iterates, making the nature of convergence more explicit.

The framework uses dual smoothing and a strategy for choosing prox-centers. With these choices, it includes augmented Lagrangian, alternating direction, and dual fast-gradient methods as special cases. The stated rates apply within those cases. The contribution therefore provides both optimization methods and a common analytical framework connecting several established approaches to constrained convex minimization.
neurips-2014-constrained-convex-minimiza.tldr: A unified primal-dual framework gives optimal convergence rates separately for objective error and constraint violation.

paragraphs: Visual recognition benefits from image representations that remain stable under particular transformations. This paper builds that goal into a convolutional network through a reproducing kernel. The kernel encodes the desired invariance, and the network learns to approximate its feature map using training data.

This changes the role of network training: the representation is guided by the feature map of a kernel with specified invariance properties. The approach connects convolutional neural networks with kernel methods, giving the architecture a mathematical target for what its representation should preserve. The authors report that this produces simple architectures with accuracy similar to more complex networks, while being easy to train and robust to overfitting.

The evaluation covers digit recognition on MNIST and visual recognition on CIFAR-10 and STL-10. Reported accuracy is competitive with the state of the art on these tasks. The findings support kernel feature approximation as a useful way to construct convolutional representations, combining an explicit treatment of invariance with competitive empirical recognition performance.
neurips-2014-convolutional-kernel-networ.tldr: Convolutional kernel networks learn kernel feature maps that encode invariance, achieving competitive visual recognition with simple architectures.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to summarize a long, high-dimensional signal with a function containing k linear pieces. Its streaming approach processes the data in one pass while retaining a coreset: a compact representation tailored to preserve information needed for segmentation. Such a summary supports later analysis without retaining the entire stream.

The stated representation has size O(k log n / ε²), where n is the number of points and ε controls approximation accuracy. It approximates the sum of squared distances to any candidate k-piecewise linear function within a factor of 1 + ε. This bound is independent of signal dimension and grows only logarithmically with stream length, while scaling linearly with the number of segments.

The authors also show that these coresets can be constructed through parallel streaming. Their analysis connects statistical estimation with computational geometry. Experiments use large synthetic and real datasets from GPS, video, and finance, with computation distributed across 255 cloud machines. The contribution combines a compactness guarantee with a construction suitable for streaming and parallel processing.
neurips-2014-coresets-for-k-segmentation.tldr: Compact streaming coresets preserve segmentation costs with a formal approximation guarantee and support parallel construction.

paragraphs: Clustering often comes with limits on how many data points each cluster may contain. These capacity constraints create the balanced clustering problem, where assignments must respect cluster sizes as well as the clustering objective. The paper addresses this problem for large datasets in metric spaces, with computation distributed across machines.

The proposed framework is based on mapping coresets. It uses this representation to develop distributed algorithms for a broad range of clustering objectives, including k-center, k-median, and k-means. A central requirement is to retain guarantees for the capacity-constrained problem while organizing the computation in distributed form.

The resulting algorithms match the best known single-machine approximation ratios for the objectives covered. An approximation ratio measures how the returned solution compares with an optimal solution, so this result preserves established solution-quality guarantees in the distributed setting. The contribution is a general theoretical framework spanning several clustering objectives, giving distributed balanced clustering a foundation comparable to that available for single-machine algorithms.
neurips-2014-distributed-balanced-cluste.tldr: Mapping coresets enable distributed balanced clustering with approximation ratios matching the best known single-machine guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies online learning when choosing an action reveals its loss and possibly the losses of other actions. Which additional losses become visible depends on the chosen action and a directed observation system selected by the environment. This creates a feedback setting between ordinary bandit feedback and observing every action's loss.

The first algorithm achieves near-optimal regret guarantees without knowing the observation system before choosing an action. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a comparison choice. The result therefore provides a strong learning guarantee despite uncertainty about which side observations the current decision will reveal.

The authors also introduce a combinatorial setting with feedback between semi-bandit and full information. Because the first algorithm's predictions are not always efficiently computable there, they develop a second algorithm with similar properties and guaranteed computational efficiency, at the cost of more complicated tuning. Both use implicit exploration, a new strategy shown to improve computational and information-theoretic efficiency over previously studied exploration strategies for the problem.
neurips-2014-efficient-learning-by-impli.tldr: Implicit exploration gives efficient learning with strong regret guarantees when actions reveal extra losses through an initially unknown observation system.

paragraphs: A predictor deployed in a production system can change the features it later uses to make predictions. For example, predicting a behavior may help cause that behavior, creating a self-fulfilling pattern. The paper studies how to detect this feedback when a predictive model is already operating within a live system.

The authors formulate feedback detection as a causal inference problem. The question concerns whether the deployed predictor influences its inputs, making the direction of influence central to the analysis. They introduce a local randomization scheme designed to detect nonlinear feedback, extending the proposed detection approach to relationships that need not follow a simple linear pattern.

The methodology is examined in a pilot study involving a predictive system deployed within a search engine. This provides an application of the proposed causal approach in a real production setting. The paper's contribution is a way to investigate whether a live predictor participates in creating the signals it subsequently observes, with the pilot study illustrating its practical use.
neurips-2014-feedback-detection-for-live.tldr: A causal inference approach uses local randomization to detect nonlinear feedback from deployed predictors into their own input features.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning algorithms can spend many samples estimating transition probabilities accurately, even when that accuracy has little relevance to future value. If an action only leads to states with the same value, the exact probabilities among those destinations do not matter for that value calculation. The paper uses this observation to reconsider how difficulty should be measured.

The authors introduce the distribution-norm, which captures variation in a function under a probability measure. They establish a concentration inequality for its dual, providing an alternative to the generic L1 concentration bounds used in many reinforcement learning analyses. This allows those analyses to reflect features of a problem that generic transition-error measures can overlook.

Several common reinforcement learning benchmarks have low hardness under the new measure. The result suggests that state count and diameter can miss distinctions relevant to learning difficulty. The contribution provides a finer way to assess a Markov decision process by accounting for how transition uncertainty interacts with variation in the quantities being estimated.
neurips-2014-how-hard-is-my-mdp-the-dist.tldr: The distribution-norm measures MDP difficulty more finely by capturing when accurate transition probabilities matter for value estimation.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning labels for graph vertices through embeddings on a unit sphere. It focuses on orthonormal representations and proves that statistically consistent representations exist for a large class of graphs, including power-law and random graphs. This addresses a theoretical question about which embeddings can support reliable learning as the problem grows.

The analysis extends statistical consistency from inductive learning to graph transduction, where the graph supplies the vertices whose labels are to be inferred. It relates Rademacher complexity to structural graph properties such as chromatic number. The authors also state an Ω((ϑ(G)/n)^(1/4)) lower bound on the required labeled fraction, connecting label requirements to the Lovász theta function and graph connectivity.

The framework extends to learning from multiple graphs representing different views of the same problem. This supplies statistical understanding for the heuristic of combining graph Laplacians through a convex combination. Together, the results connect representation choice, graph structure, and labeled sample requirements, while establishing existence of suitable representations across the stated graph classes.
neurips-2014-learning-on-graphs-using-or.tldr: The paper proves existence of statistically consistent graph embeddings and connects labeled sample requirements to graph structure.

paragraphs: Aligning multivariate time series means identifying which positions in one sequence correspond to positions in another. The quality of that alignment depends on how differences between observations are measured. This paper learns a Mahalanobis distance from training sequences whose correct alignments are known, using supervision to adapt the similarity measure to the task.

The authors formulate alignment as structured prediction, treating the correspondence between sequences as the output to be learned. They propose losses that measure errors between alignments while keeping optimization tractable. This connects the learned distance to the quality of the resulting sequence alignment, rather than leaving similarity as a fixed input to the procedure.

Experiments on real audio-to-audio data show improved alignment performance from learning the similarity measure. The paper also uses the framework for feature selection, combining basic audio features into a representation with better alignment performance. These findings support learning both how observations are compared and which features contribute to that comparison from examples of correct temporal correspondence.
neurips-2014-metric-learning-for-tempora.tldr: Learning a distance from known temporal alignments improves audio sequence alignment and supports feature selection.

paragraphs: An f-divergence measures a difference between probability distributions, but estimating it from samples also requires understanding estimation uncertainty. A mean squared error rate describes average estimation accuracy without fully specifying the estimator's distribution. This paper addresses that additional question for a previously proposed ensemble estimator of multivariate f-divergence.

The authors establish asymptotic normality: as the sample size grows, an appropriately normalized estimation error approaches a normal distribution. The estimator already has a mean squared error rate of O(1/T), is simple to implement, and is reported to perform well in high dimensions. The new theory adds distributional information that makes the estimator useful for statistical inference.

One resulting application is testing whether two sample sets come from the same distribution. The authors experimentally validate the theoretical findings and illustrate their use by empirically bounding the best achievable classification error. The contribution thus connects divergence estimation with uncertainty-aware decisions, allowing estimated distributional differences to support inference tasks beyond producing a single numerical value.
neurips-2014-multivariate-f-divergence-e.tldr: An asymptotic normality result turns an ensemble f-divergence estimator into a tool for distribution testing and classification-error analysis.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to study neural networks through relationships between spike trains and local field potentials recorded across brain regions. Its target is connectivity patterns that vary with time and frequency. Such patterns provide a way to characterize neural networks within the broader goal of relating them to behavior, environments, or genotypes.

The method uses convolutional dictionary learning to connect the two types of recordings. It models dynamic spike-LFP relationships and examines how well spikes from across the brain predict local field potential data in a particular region. This predictive formulation gives a concrete way to analyze relationships among signals observed in different locations.

The authors also develop a clustering method for inferring similarities among neurons from multiple regions. Their results use simultaneous spike and local field potential recordings from as many as sixteen regions in a mouse. The contribution combines dynamic modeling, cross-region prediction, and neuron clustering into a strategy for describing distributed neural relationships through jointly recorded activity.
neurips-2014-on-the-relations-of-lfps-ne.tldr: Convolutional dictionary learning links spikes and local field potentials to characterize dynamic relationships across brain regions.

paragraphs: The paper develops a parallel sampling method for hierarchical Dirichlet process models. Its central focus is convergence: how effectively the sampler explores the model's possible configurations. The proposed method builds on an earlier sampling approach by using learned sub-clusters to construct large split and merge proposals.

These proposals let the sampler consider substantial changes to its clustering configuration, including additional global splits and merges. Learned sub-clusters guide those changes, providing structure for the proposed rearrangements. In the reported experiments, adding the global moves drastically improves convergence. This supports the use of broader, informed proposals as a way to improve sampling for these hierarchical models.

The paper also examines how convergence is assessed. The authors find that cross-validation techniques do not adequately determine convergence and that previous sampling methods converge more slowly than had been expected. These findings affect how the experimental improvements should be understood: evaluating a sampler requires attention to its convergence behavior, and cross-validation alone was insufficient for that purpose in their investigation.
neurips-2014-parallel-sampling-of-hdps-u.tldr: Parallel HDP sampling with learned split and merge proposals improves experimental convergence and exposes shortcomings in cross-validation-based convergence assessment.

paragraphs: The paper models event data whose rate changes among an unknown number of states. It starts with an inhomogeneous Poisson process and uses a Chinese restaurant process to modify its rate. This provides a probabilistic framework for representing discrete rate states while leaving their number to be inferred from observations.

The authors apply an MCMC sampler to perform posterior Bayesian inference. The resulting task includes estimating how many states are supported by Poisson-like data, so uncertainty about the state count becomes part of the model's inference problem. This is useful for the paper's focus on signals whose changing event frequency may be represented through distinct underlying rates.

On synthetic data, the sampler is reported to produce accurate results. The authors then apply the model to spike recordings from V1 neurons, identifying discrete firing-rate states that depend on stimulus orientation. This application connects the general rate-switching model to neural activity, using observed spike events to investigate how firing states relate to the presented stimulus.
neurips-2014-poisson-process-jumping-bet.tldr: A Bayesian Poisson-process model infers an unknown number of rate states and is applied to orientation-dependent neural firing.

paragraphs: The paper proposes initializing a recurrent neural network using a linear autoencoder trained on sequences. These autoencoders are linear dynamical systems that model the target sequences. The approach uses what the simpler sequence model learns to provide initial weights before the recurrent network is trained for its intended task.

The authors first derive a closed-form solution for the optimal linear autoencoder weights given a training set. Computing that solution is very demanding, so they introduce a procedure that approximates it for a specified number of hidden units. The resulting weights initialize the recurrent network's input-to-hidden connections, linking the sequence autoencoder directly to the later training process.

Evaluation uses four established datasets of polyphonic music sequences. The authors report large improvements over the state of the art on all four datasets. These findings support the effectiveness of the proposed initialization in the tested sequence tasks. The contribution combines an analytical characterization of the linear autoencoder with a practical approximation and an empirical demonstration of its value for recurrent network pre-training.
neurips-2014-pre-training-of-recurrent-n.tldr: Linear sequence autoencoders provide effective recurrent-network initialization, substantially improving results on four polyphonic music datasets.

paragraphs: MCMC methods can sample from a wide range of distributions, but reaching the stationary distribution may take a long or uncertain amount of time. This paper addresses that difficulty for univariate Gibbs sampling in Markov random fields. It gives sufficient conditions on model parameters that guarantee fast mixing in a precise mathematical sense.

The authors then provide an algorithm for Euclidean projection onto the parameter set satisfying those conditions. Projection supplies a way to move model parameters into a region where the mixing guarantee applies. The conditions are sufficient, so the identified region is a certified set of fast-mixing parameters rather than a claim that every fast-mixing model must belong to it.

The paper also illustrates projection using various divergence measures. It compares univariate marginals obtained by sampling after projection with common variational methods and Gibbs sampling using the original parameters. This connects the theoretical guarantee to an inference comparison: changing parameters affects the distribution being sampled, while placing the sampling process within the stated fast-mixing conditions.
neurips-2014-projecting-markov-random-fi.tldr: The paper gives sufficient fast-mixing conditions for Gibbs sampling and an algorithm that projects MRF parameters into the guaranteed region.

paragraphs: Metric labeling assigns labels while balancing individual assignment costs against pairwise costs based on distances between labels. It is a form of energy minimization for pairwise Markov random fields. The paper connects two established solution approaches: iterative move-making through minimum cuts and linear programming relaxations followed by randomized rounding.

A relaxed linear program can produce fractional assignments, which rounding converts into discrete labels. The authors consider a large class of parallel rounding procedures and design move-making algorithms that closely imitate them. This creates a systematic correspondence between how a fractional solution is rounded and how an iterative algorithm changes a discrete labeling.

They prove that each constructed move-making algorithm has a multiplicative bound exactly matching the approximation factor of its corresponding rounding procedure, for arbitrary distance functions within the stated result. Their analysis includes all known move-making results as special cases. The contribution therefore unifies existing guarantees and provides a route for designing move-making methods from rounding procedures with understood approximation behavior.
neurips-2014-rounding-based-moves-for-me.tldr: Move-making algorithms derived from rounding procedures inherit exactly matching approximation guarantees for metric labeling.

paragraphs: The paper studies exact recovery of a polynomial on Boolean inputs with at most s nonzero coefficients. Examples are drawn uniformly at random. The proposed algorithm runs in time polynomial in n and 2^s, where n is the input dimension, and succeeds under a sufficient condition called the unique sign property.

That property requires an output value associated with a unique configuration of the participating parities. The authors describe circumstances supporting it, including small random coefficient perturbations, randomly chosen parities, and positive coefficients, with the stated probabilistic qualifications. This explains how a problem considered difficult in the worst case can become tractable for almost all sparse polynomials in their analysis. The runtime still depends on 2^s.

The authors apply the recovery result to hypergraph sketching, learning a hypergraph from uniformly sampled random cuts. The targeted hypergraphs are sparse both in their number of hyperedges and in hyperedge size. They also report experiments on a real-world dataset, connecting the conditional polynomial-learning result to recovering sparse graph-like structure from random observations.
neurips-2014-sparse-polynomial-learning-.tldr: A sufficient uniqueness condition enables exact sparse-polynomial recovery from random examples, with an application to hypergraph sketching.

paragraphs: The paper asks how difficult it is to recover the graph underlying a discrete undirected graphical model from independent samples. For general models with p nodes and maximum degree d, it establishes an unconditional Ω(p^(d/2)) computational lower bound for a specified class of statistical algorithms. The construction connects this difficulty to learning parities with noise.

This lower bound shows that substantial improvements over exhaustive search require restrictions on the model class within the scope of the result. The paper then investigates antiferromagnetic models, where interactions are repelling. Its findings reveal a setting in which strong interactions can make structure learning computationally easier.

For a class of these models, sufficiently strong repulsion permits learning in approximately quadratic time, expressed as Õ(p²). The proposed algorithm's performance ranges between Õ(p²) and Õ(p^(d+2)), depending on repulsion strength. The two contributions together distinguish general computational hardness from the favorable behavior available in a particular model family, showing that interaction type and strength can be central to learning complexity.
neurips-2014-structure-learning-of-antif.tldr: General graphical-model learning has a strong computational lower bound, while strong repulsion enables efficient learning for a class of antiferromagnetic models.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression can be accelerated by summarizing observations with a smaller pseudo-dataset. Maintaining accuracy across a wider input range, however, can require more pseudo-points. This is problematic for time-series and spatial data because computation in typical approaches grows quadratically with the pseudo-dataset size.

The paper constructs an approximation whose complexity grows linearly with the number of pseudo-points. It imposes a tree or chain structure on those points and calibrates the approximation through Kullback-Leibler minimization. The structure allows inference and learning to use Gaussian belief propagation efficiently, changing how the computational cost scales as the summary grows.

The authors evaluate the approach on challenging regression tasks, including missing-data imputation for audio and spatial datasets. They examine the speed-accuracy trade-off and report a frontier that dominates those of many existing approximation methods. These findings support the practical value of the structured approximation in the tested tasks, especially where retaining enough pseudo-points is important for accuracy over a broad input range.
neurips-2014-tree-structured-gaussian-pr.tldr: Tree-structured pseudo-data make Gaussian process approximation scale linearly in summary size and improve the reported speed-accuracy trade-off.

paragraphs: The paper addresses abstract planning when reward functions can change at any time. An option represents an extended course of action whose expected return must be evaluated for the current task. The authors introduce a universal option model that is independent of the reward function, allowing the learned model to be reused as rewards change.

They prove that a universal option model can construct a traditional option model once rewards are specified. An option's conditional expected return can be computed directly with a single dot product. They extend the framework to linear function approximation, establish its connection to temporal-difference solutions, and provide an incremental learning algorithm with a consistency proof.

Applications include document recommendation, where each query defines rewards for a simulated walk through references, and a real-time strategy game with dynamically specified tasks. Experiments report substantially more efficient evaluation of option returns and policies than previously known methods. The contribution separates learning reusable option models from evaluating particular rewards, supporting rapid reassessment when planning objectives change.
neurips-2014-universal-option-models-0e5.tldr: Universal option models reuse reward-independent information to evaluate changing planning objectives efficiently, including through a single dot product.

paragraphs: The paper develops unsupervised local learning rules for recurrent networks that represent both current inputs and their recent history. Its main theory concerns linear networks. The aim is to learn useful short-term memory through updates based on local information, with an explicit cost function connecting the rules to efficient representation.

The recurrent-weight rule drives the network toward a regime where recurrent inputs cancel feedforward signal inputs on average. The authors show that this rule minimizes a cost. Once recurrent activity predicts feedforward input, a separate rule for feedforward weights reduces the cost further. They also modify the rules to accommodate non-whitened inputs directly.

Applying the learning rules to a network that receives a delayed version of its own output leads it to represent both incoming signals and their history. This links the predictive cancellation mechanism to memory formation. The authors additionally sketch how the rules could transfer to balanced spiking networks; that extension is presented as a possible transfer beyond the developed linear-network theory.
neurips-2014-unsupervised-learning-of-an.tldr: Local unsupervised learning rules train linear recurrent networks to efficiently represent present inputs and their history.
